questions.question: An order has 3 lines and 2 payments. Joining orders, order_items and payments gives how many rows for it?
questions.explain: Each line pairs with each payment: 3 × 2 = 6. Sums over either side are inflated.

questions.question: What is the reliable fix for fan-out?

options.b: Aggregate each detail table to the report grain, then join
options.c: Use LEFT JOIN instead of JOIN

questions.section: 3. The fix: aggregate each fact to the grain, then join
questions.explain: Summaries at the same grain join one-to-one. DISTINCT breaks when two real amounts are equal.

questions.question: A customer has no paid orders. How do you keep them in a per-customer report?

options.a: Start from customers and LEFT JOIN the summaries, with COALESCE
options.c: Filter WHERE revenue IS NOT NULL

questions.explain: The entity table drives the report; missing facts become 0 through COALESCE.

questions.question: How can you detect inflated totals?

options.a: Compare the report's grand total with the source table's total
options.b: Check the query runs without errors

questions.section: 5. Verify: totals must survive the reshaping
questions.explain: Reshaping must not change the grand total. A mismatch reveals fan-out or lost rows.

questions.question: Why does `employee_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees)` return no rows?
questions.section: 2. IN subqueries: a list of values
questions.explain: x NOT IN (…, NULL) is unknown for every x that isn't in the list, so nothing passes WHERE.

questions.question: What does a scalar subquery return when it finds no rows?
questions.explain: An empty scalar subquery evaluates to NULL.

questions.question: A correlated subquery…

options.a: runs once for the whole query
options.b: refers to a column of the outer query's current row

questions.explain: It is logically evaluated per outer row, using that row's values.

questions.question: What must a derived table (subquery in FROM) have?
questions.section: 3. Derived tables: a subquery in FROM
questions.explain: You refer to its columns through the alias: (SELECT …) AS s.

questions.question: What does the subquery of EXISTS usually select?
questions.section: 1. EXISTS: is there at least one?
questions.explain: EXISTS ignores the selected columns; SELECT 1 states that clearly.

questions.question: A customer has three pending orders. `WHERE EXISTS (…pending…)` returns them…
questions.section: 1. EXISTS: is there at least one?
questions.explain: EXISTS is a semi-join: it filters outer rows and never duplicates them.

questions.question: Why is NOT EXISTS safer than NOT IN?

options.b: It's never unknown, so NULLs can't empty the result

questions.section: 3. Why NOT EXISTS beats NOT IN
questions.explain: EXISTS returns only true or false.

questions.question: Where does the condition `o.status = 'paid'` go in "products not in any paid order"?
questions.explain: It describes which related rows count; outside, it would refer to nothing or change the question.

questions.question: How long does a CTE exist?

options.b: For the one statement it's defined in

questions.explain: Use a view for a reusable named query.

questions.question: How are several CTEs written?

options.a: WITH a AS (…), b AS (…) SELECT …
options.b: WITH a AS (…) WITH b AS (…) SELECT …

questions.explain: One WITH, then comma-separated definitions; later ones can use earlier ones.

questions.question: Do CTEs make queries faster?

options.c: Not necessarily: write them for clarity

questions.explain: The optimiser may inline or materialise them. Measure if speed matters.

questions.question: A stage should be one row per order, but `COUNT(*)` ≠ `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)`. What does that mean?

options.a: The stage is not at the grain you think

questions.explain: Duplicate keys in a stage mean a join or grouping is at the wrong grain.

questions.question: Which branch of a CASE wins when several are true?
questions.explain: Branches are tested top to bottom; order them from most specific to broadest.

questions.question: What does a CASE without ELSE return when nothing matches?
questions.explain: Decide explicitly with ELSE what an unmatched row should get.

questions.question: `COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts…
questions.section: 3. Conditional aggregation: many counts in one pass
questions.explain: 0 is not NULL, so COUNT counts it. Use SUM(… ELSE 0) or COUNT(… END) without ELSE.

questions.question: Why keep a total column next to pivoted method columns?

options.a: To detect values none of the branches cover

questions.explain: If the method columns don't add up to the total, a new or unexpected value exists.

questions.question: How does `AVG(x) OVER (PARTITION BY team_id)` differ from `GROUP BY team_id`?

options.a: It keeps every row and adds the team average to each

questions.explain: Window functions compute across related rows without collapsing them.

questions.question: Salaries 100, 90, 90, 80. What does RANK give the 80?
questions.explain: RANK skips after ties (1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE_RANK would give 3.

questions.question: Why can't you write `WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (…) <= 2`?

options.a: WHERE runs before window functions are computed

questions.explain: Compute the number in a CTE or subquery and filter in the outer query.

questions.question: What does `SUM(revenue_cents) OVER ()` return on each row?

options.b: The grand total of all rows

questions.explain: An empty OVER () makes the whole result one window.

questions.question: What does LAG return on the first row of a partition?

options.c: NULL, unless you give a default

questions.explain: There is no previous row; LAG(x, 1, default) supplies a value instead.

questions.question: Monthly rows skip a month with no sales. What does LAG(revenue) compare with?

options.b: The previous row, i.e. two months back

questions.explain: LAG works on rows, not calendars. Generate a complete calendar first.

questions.question: Which frame gives a three-row moving average?

options.a: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

questions.explain: Two previous rows plus the current one.

questions.question: Two rows share the same ORDER BY value. With the default frame, their running totals are…

options.a: different, one step at a time
options.b: equal, because RANGE treats ties as one step

questions.section: 5. ROWS vs RANGE: the duplicate trap
questions.explain: The default frame is RANGE … CURRENT ROW, which includes all peers. Make the order unique or use ROWS.

questions.question: Which filter covers all of June 2026, even for timestamps?
questions.explain: A half-open range never misses the last day's later hours or double-counts a boundary.

questions.question: `strftime('%m', '2026-03-12') = 3` is…

options.b: false, because strftime returns the text '03'

questions.explain: Compare with '03' or CAST the result to INTEGER.

questions.question: What is `date('2026-01-31', '+1 month')` in SQLite?
questions.explain: SQLite normalises February 31 to March 3. Test month-end arithmetic.

questions.question: How do you get the number of days between two ISO dates?
questions.explain: Subtracting text doesn't give days; julianday turns dates into day numbers.

questions.question: What's the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?

options.a: UNION removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL keeps them

questions.explain: UNION ALL is cheaper and keeps genuine repeats; use UNION only when you need de-duplication.

questions.question: Set operations match columns…
questions.explain: The first SELECT's names are used; values line up by position.

questions.question: Which keeps rows of the first query that are not in the second?
questions.section: 4. EXCEPT: in the first, not the second
questions.explain: EXCEPT is set difference.

questions.question: To prove a rewritten query returns the same rows, run EXCEPT…

options.b: in both directions, and compare counts

questions.section: 5. EXCEPT as a test: do two queries agree?
questions.explain: One direction misses extra rows in the other; counts catch duplicate differences.

questions.question: A view…

options.a: stores a copy of the rows
options.b: stores the query and recomputes it when read
options.c: is deleted at the end of the statement

questions.section: 2. A view stores the query, not the rows
questions.explain: A snapshot table stores rows; a view always reflects current data.

questions.question: After `ROLLBACK TO my_savepoint`, the transaction is…
questions.section: 4. Savepoints: undo part of the work
questions.explain: Only the work after the savepoint is undone; you still need COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

questions.question: Why should transactions be short?

options.b: Open transactions hold locks that make other writers wait

questions.explain: SQLite allows one writer at a time; PostgreSQL long transactions hold row locks and block clean-up.

questions.question: Two requests read stock = 1 and both write stock = 0. What prevents selling the item twice?

options.b: A conditional UPDATE … WHERE stock >= 1 and checking rows changed

questions.explain: Make the write itself check the condition, so only one request can succeed.
